The fluid rotation associated with a vortex can be parameterized by the circulation $\Gamma=\oint {\rm d}{\bf r}\cdot{\bf v}({\bf r})$ about the vortex, where ${\bf v}({\bf r})$ is the fluid velocity field. While classical vortices can take any value of circulation, superfluids are irrotational, and any rotation or angular momentum is constrained to occur through vortices with quantized circulation. In addition to BECs, quantized vortices also occur in superfluid Helium, nonlinear optics, and type-II superconductors.

# Vortices in Classical and Superfluid Systems

Vortices represent the breakdown of laminar fluid flow and therefore play a key role in turbulence throughout nature. When smooth, orderly fluid motion becomes unstable, it gives way to the swirling, rotational structures we recognize as vortices. These structures are fundamental to understanding turbulent phenomena, which appear across an enormous range of scales—from the eddies in a flowing stream to the vast atmospheric systems that shape planetary weather.

The rotational character of a vortex is quantified by its circulation, defined as

$$\Gamma=\oint {\rm d}{\bf r}\cdot{\bf v}({\bf r}),$$

where the integral is taken around a closed loop enclosing the vortex and ${\bf v}({\bf r})$ is the fluid velocity field. This quantity captures the net "swirl" of the flow around the vortex core and serves as the primary parameter characterizing vortex rotation.

A striking distinction emerges when comparing classical fluids to superfluids. In classical systems, the circulation can take on any continuous value, reflecting the smooth range of rotational states available to an ordinary fluid. Superfluids, however, are irrotational, and this fundamental property restricts rotation to a discrete set of possibilities. Rather than rotating as a whole, a superfluid can only accommodate rotation through vortices whose circulation is quantized, taking values that are integer multiples of a fundamental quantum set by the mass of the constituent particles.

These quantized vortices have been observed experimentally in Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs) in a variety of forms. Depending on the conditions, they can appear as isolated single vortices, as ordered arrays known as vortex lattices, and as more complex configurations such as vortex pairs and vortex rings. The rich phenomenology of these structures has made BECs an ideal platform for studying quantized vorticity in a controlled setting.

The significance of quantized vortices extends beyond bosonic systems. The observation of quantized vortices in a fermionic gas provided clear and compelling evidence of the underlying condensation and superfluidity of fermion pairs. Because individual fermions cannot condense directly, the emergence of quantized vortices demonstrated that the fermions had paired up and formed a coherent superfluid state, offering direct confirmation of pairing and macroscopic quantum coherence in these systems.

# Quantized Vortices in Superfluid Systems

Vortices are ubiquitous in nature, appearing across an extraordinary range of physical scales—from the swirling patterns of water draining from a basin to the vast rotating storms in planetary atmospheres and the turbulent eddies that stir interstellar gas. These rotational structures are far from mere curiosities; they play a central role in the physics of turbulence and govern how energy, momentum, and other conserved quantities are transported and ultimately dissipated within a fluid. In classical fluids, vortices can possess arbitrary values of circulation, and their formation, interaction, and decay underlie some of the most challenging unsolved problems in physics, including the nature of fully developed turbulence.

Superfluids occupy a distinctive place in this broader landscape. Because a superfluid is described by a single macroscopic wavefunction with a well-defined phase, its velocity field is proportional to the gradient of that phase and is therefore fundamentally irrotational. This constraint has a profound consequence: rotation cannot be accommodated smoothly throughout the fluid as it can in an ordinary liquid. Instead, all rotational motion must be concentrated into discrete, topologically protected line defects known as quantized vortices. Around each such vortex, the circulation Γ is not continuous but restricted to integer multiples of a fundamental quantum, Γ = h/m, where h is Planck's constant and m is the mass of the relevant particle or pair. At the core of each vortex, the superfluid density vanishes, and the phase of the wavefunction winds by a multiple of 2π, giving these objects their characteristic quantized nature.

The remarkable universality of this phenomenon is reflected in the wide variety of systems in which quantized vortices have been directly observed. They appear in dilute atomic Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs), where they can be created and imaged with exquisite control; in ultracold fermionic gases, where the underlying condensation arises from paired atoms; and in superfluid Helium, the original and archetypal quantum liquid in which quantized circulation was first predicted and later confirmed. Beyond these atomic and cryogenic settings, analogous quantized vortices emerge in nonlinear optical systems, where light propagating through a nonlinear medium can behave as a photon fluid, and in type-II superconductors, where magnetic flux threads the material in the form of quantized vortex lines within the superconducting condensate.

Across all of these diverse physical platforms, the appearance of quantized vortices carries deep significance. Their very existence, along with the discrete and quantized nature of their circulation, serves as an unambiguous signature of the underlying macroscopic quantum coherence—that is, of condensation and superfluidity itself. In this way, quantized vortices act both as fundamental building blocks of quantum turbulence and as direct experimental hallmarks of the exotic quantum states that host them.

# Vortices and the Role of Gamma

Vortices are among the most fascinating structures in fluid dynamics, appearing everywhere from the swirling water in a draining sink to the massive spiral arms of hurricanes and galaxies. At their core, vortices represent regions where fluid rotates around a central axis, creating patterns of motion that are both beautiful and mathematically rich.

## Understanding the Vortex

The defining feature of any vortex is its rotational motion. As fluid particles circle around the vortex center, they establish a flow field that can be described precisely using the mathematical language of vector calculus. The strength and behavior of a vortex depend on several factors, including the speed of rotation, the size of the rotating region, and the properties of the surrounding fluid.

Vortices come in many forms. Some are stable and long-lived, persisting for extended periods while maintaining their shape. Others are transient, forming and dissipating quickly as energy disperses through the fluid. The study of these structures helps scientists and engineers understand phenomena ranging from aircraft wake turbulence to ocean currents.

## The Significance of Gamma

In the mathematical treatment of vortices, the Greek letter Gamma (Γ) holds special importance. It represents **circulation**, a quantity that measures the total "amount of rotation" around a closed loop in the fluid. Circulation is calculated by integrating the velocity of the fluid along a closed path, and it provides a powerful way to quantify the intensity of a vortex.

The concept of Gamma is central to many foundational principles in fluid mechanics. For example, Kelvin's circulation theorem states that, under certain ideal conditions, the circulation around a fluid loop remains constant over time. This conservation principle helps explain why vortices tend to persist and why they behave in predictable ways.

Gamma also connects directly to the lift generated by airplane wings. The Kutta-Joukowski theorem relates the lift force on an object to the circulation around it, demonstrating how a seemingly abstract mathematical quantity has profound real-world consequences.

## Conclusion

The interplay between vortices and the circulation parameter Gamma illustrates how elegant mathematics can capture the complexity of natural phenomena. By quantifying rotation through Gamma, scientists gain the tools to predict, analyze, and harness the power of swirling flows—whether designing more efficient aircraft, forecasting weather patterns, or exploring the fundamental behavior of fluids in motion.

# Quantized Vortices in Bose-Einstein Condensates

Vortices are among the most striking manifestations of quantum mechanics at a macroscopic scale, representing topological defects around which the quantum-mechanical phase of a system winds by an integer multiple of $2\pi$. In classical fluids, a vortex is a region of rotating flow—familiar from everyday phenomena such as whirlpools, tornadoes, and the swirling water draining from a bathtub—where the fluid circulates around a central core. In quantum fluids, however, this circulation is not continuous but *quantized*: the flow around the vortex core can only take discrete values set by fundamental constants, a direct consequence of the requirement that the macroscopic wavefunction be single-valued. Such quantized vortices arise in a variety of coherent quantum systems, including superfluid helium, superconductors (where they appear as magnetic flux lines), and, most controllably, in dilute-gas Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs). First realized experimentally in 1995 by cooling dilute atomic gases to nanokelvin temperatures, BECs provide a remarkably clean and tunable platform for studying vortex physics, as their low densities, weak interactions, and optical accessibility allow vortices to be created, imaged, and manipulated with unprecedented precision. In these systems, vortices typically emerge when the condensate is set into rotation—for example, by "stirring" the atomic cloud with laser beams or rotating an anisotropic trapping potential—organizing themselves into ordered arrays known as Abrikosov lattices when their number grows large. The study of these quantized vortices offers deep insight into superfluidity, quantum turbulence, and the fundamental nature of coherence in interacting many-body quantum systems.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the concept of circulation and how quantized vortices differ between classical fluids and superfluids.
counterfactuals.output:
# Circulation and Quantized Vortices

## What is Circulation?

**Circulation** (Γ) is a measure of the "amount of rotation" in a fluid around a closed loop. Mathematically, it's defined as the line integral of the velocity field around a closed path:

$$\Gamma = \oint_C \vec{v} \cdot d\vec{l}$$

Physically, it quantifies how much the fluid tends to circulate along a given contour. If you imagine placing a tiny paddle wheel in the flow, circulation relates to whether and how strongly it would spin.

---

## Vortices in Classical Fluids

In an ordinary (classical) fluid like water or air:

- **Circulation can take any value** — it's a continuous quantity
- A vortex (like a whirlpool or tornado) can have any strength of rotation
- The velocity typically follows a profile where the fluid spins faster near the core
- Circulation can be gradually created, destroyed, or changed
- The vortex core can have any size and the rotation "smears out" continuously

The key feature: **there is no fundamental restriction on the circulation value.**

---

## Vortices in Superfluids

Superfluids (such as liquid helium-4 below ~2.17 K, or ultracold atomic gases) behave dramatically differently due to their **quantum-mechanical nature**.

### The Origin: A Macroscopic Wavefunction

A superfluid is described by a single, coherent quantum wavefunction:

$$\psi = |\psi| \, e^{i\phi}$$

The fluid velocity is directly tied to the **gradient of the phase** (φ):

$$\vec{v} = \frac{\hbar}{m} \nabla \phi$$

### Quantization of Circulation

Because the wavefunction must be **single-valued**, the phase can only change by integer multiples of 2π around any closed loop. This forces the circulation to be **quantized**:

$$\Gamma = \oint \vec{v} \cdot d\vec{l} = n\frac{h}{m}, \quad n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

where:
- **h** = Planck's constant
- **m** = mass of the fluid particle (e.g., a helium atom)
- **n** = an integer (the quantum number)

---

## Key Differences Summarized

| Feature | Classical Fluid | Superfluid |
|---------|----------------|------------|
| **Circulation values** | Continuous (any value) | Discrete (quantized in units of h/m) |
| **Vortex strength** | Arbitrary | Fixed multiples of the quantum |
| **Core** | Can be any size, viscous | Tiny, well-defined; density → 0 |
| **Rotation of bulk** | Whole fluid rotates | Fluid stays irrotational except at vortex lines |
| **Origin** | Classical hydrodynamics | Quantum phase coherence |

---

## Physical Consequences

1. **Vortex arrays:** When you rotate a container of superfluid, instead of the whole fluid rotating rigidly, it forms a **regular lattice of quantized vortices**, each carrying exactly one quantum of circulation.

2. **Stability:** A single vortex with n = 1 is generally more stable than one large vortex with high n, which tends to split into multiple singly-quantized vortices.

3. **Irrotational flow:** Between vortices, the superfluid remains perfectly irrotational — all the "rotation" is concentrated in discrete, thread-like vortex lines.

---

## The Big Picture

The quantization of vortices is one of the most striking **macroscopic manifestations of quantum mechanics**. While quantum effects are usually confined to the atomic scale, here we see a quantum constraint governing the behavior of a fluid you could, in principle, observe directly — a beautiful example of quantum physics operating at a visible scale.

Would you like me to go deeper into any aspect, such as the mathematics of the vortex lattice or experimental observations?

# Vortices in Turbulence, Superfluids, and Quantum Gases

## Introduction

Vortices represent one of the most ubiquitous and fascinating structures in fluid dynamics, appearing across an extraordinary range of scales—from the swirling of water down a drain to the rotating storms of planetary atmospheres, and down to the microscopic quantized whirls in superfluids and ultracold quantum gases. Understanding the nature of vortices provides a unifying thread connecting classical hydrodynamics to quantum many-body physics.

## Circulation in Classical Fluids

The central quantity characterizing a vortex is its **circulation**, defined as the line integral of the velocity field around a closed contour. For a fluid with velocity field $\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r})$, the circulation $\Gamma$ around a closed loop $C$ is:

$$
\Gamma = \oint_C \mathbf{v} \cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}
$$

By Stokes' theorem, this can be equivalently expressed as a surface integral of the vorticity $\boldsymbol{\omega} = \nabla \times \mathbf{v}$ over any surface $S$ bounded by $C$:

$$
\Gamma = \int_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{v}) \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

In a classical inviscid fluid, Kelvin's circulation theorem guarantees that $\Gamma$ is conserved along the flow, endowing vortices with a robust topological character. Crucially, in a classical fluid the circulation can take *any* real value—the vorticity is a continuous field, and vortices may possess arbitrary strength.

## Turbulence

In classical turbulence, the flow is characterized by a chaotic tangle of vortices spanning a wide range of length scales. Energy injected at large scales cascades down through progressively smaller eddies until it is dissipated by viscosity at the smallest scales—a picture encapsulated by the celebrated Kolmogorov theory, which predicts an energy spectrum $E(k) \propto \epsilon^{2/3} k^{-5/3}$ in the inertial range. The continuous distribution of vortex sizes and strengths makes classical turbulence a notoriously difficult problem, and it is precisely this continuity that distinguishes it from its quantum counterpart.

## Quantized Vortices in Superfluids

The situation changes dramatically in a superfluid, such as liquid helium-4 below the lambda transition ($T_\lambda \approx 2.17$ K). Here the system is described by a macroscopic complex order parameter—a condensate wavefunction:

$$
\psi(\mathbf{r}) = |\psi(\mathbf{r})|\, e^{i\phi(\mathbf{r})}
$$

The superfluid velocity is proportional to the gradient of the phase $\phi$:

$$
\mathbf{v}_s = \frac{\hbar}{m} \nabla \phi
$$

where $m$ is the mass of the constituent particles (or pairs). Because the velocity field is the gradient of a scalar phase, the flow is irrotational ($\nabla \times \mathbf{v}_s = 0$) everywhere the wavefunction is nonzero. Vorticity can therefore only exist along singular lines where $|\psi| = 0$—the vortex cores.

The requirement that the wavefunction be single-valued imposes that the phase change around any closed loop must be an integer multiple of $2\pi$. This leads immediately to the **quantization of circulation**:

$$
\Gamma = \oint_C \mathbf{v}_s \cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell} = \frac{\hbar}{m} \oint_C \nabla\phi \cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell} = \frac{2\pi\hbar}{m}\, n = \frac{h}{m}\, n, \qquad n \in \mathbb{Z}
$$

The quantum of circulation $\kappa = h/m$ is a fundamental constant of the superfluid. Unlike classical vortices, superfluid vortices are thus discrete, topologically protected objects with quantized strength—a striking manifestation of macroscopic quantum coherence.

## Vortices in Bose–Einstein Condensates

Dilute atomic Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs) provide a remarkably clean and highly controllable platform for studying quantized vortices. Described to good approximation by the Gross–Pitaevskii equation,

$$
i\hbar \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} = \left[ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2 + V_{\text{ext}}(\mathbf{r}) + g|\psi|^2 \right]\psi,
$$

these systems exhibit the same quantization of circulation as bulk superfluids, with $\kappa = h/m$ set by the atomic mass. Vortices can be nucleated by rotating the trapping potential, by stirring with laser beams, or through the Kibble–Zurek mechanism during a rapid quench through the transition. At sufficiently high rotation rates, vortices arrange themselves into a regular triangular Abrikosov lattice, directly imaged in landmark experiments. The healing length $\xi = \hbar/\sqrt{2mg n}$ sets the size of the vortex core, providing a natural microscopic length scale.

## Vortices in Fermionic Gases

Ultracold Fermi gases extend this picture into the realm of paired superfluidity. In these systems, superfluidity arises from the condensation of fermion pairs, and the relevant mass in the circulation quantum becomes that of the pair, $2m$, giving:

$$
\Gamma = \frac{h}{2m}\, n
$$

The tunability of the interatomic interactions via Feshbach resonances allows these gases to be swept continuously across the **BEC–BCS crossover**—from a molecular BEC of tightly bound diatomic pairs, through the strongly interacting unitary regime, to the BCS limit of loosely bound, long-range Cooper pairs. The observation of vortex lattices across this entire crossover provided definitive evidence for fermionic superfluidity and demonstrated that quantized circulation persists even where the pairing is weak and the pairs are large compared to the interparticle spacing.

## Quantum Turbulence

The discreteness of superfluid vortices gives rise to **quantum turbulence**: a tangle of quantized vortex lines whose reconnections and interactions govern the flow. Because every vortex carries the same circulation $\kappa$, quantum turbulence offers a conceptually simplified—yet richly complex—analogue of its classical counterpart, in which the vorticity field is reduced to a set of discrete, identical filaments. Remarkably, under certain conditions quantum turbulence reproduces the classical Kolmogorov energy spectrum, hinting at deep connections between the quantum and classical descriptions of turbulent flow that remain an active area of research.

---

*This opening establishes the conceptual arc from classical to quantum vortices. Depending on your review's emphasis, you may wish to expand on specific experimental realizations, the mutual friction between normal and superfluid components, or the microscopic structure of vortex cores in the following sections.*

# Quantized Vortices in Superfluids

## The Role of Quantized Vortices

Quantized vortices are topological defects that play a fundamental role in the behavior of superfluids. Their key characteristics and roles include:

### Circulation Quantization
In a superfluid, the flow is described by a macroscopic wavefunction with a well-defined phase. Because this wavefunction must be single-valued, the circulation around any closed loop is quantized in units of:

$$\kappa = \frac{h}{m}$$

where *h* is Planck's constant and *m* is the mass of the constituent particle (or pair). This means angular momentum cannot be carried by smooth rotation but must be organized into discrete vortex lines.

### Accommodating Rotation
Superfluids cannot rotate like ordinary fluids because they are irrotational (zero curl of velocity almost everywhere). When forced to rotate, they respond by nucleating an array of quantized vortices—a **vortex lattice** (Abrikosov lattice)—which mimics solid-body rotation on average.

### Dissipation and Critical Velocity
Vortices govern the breakdown of superfluidity. Their motion, nucleation, and interactions with boundaries can introduce dissipation, setting critical velocities above which frictionless flow is lost.

### Quantum Turbulence
Tangles of quantized vortices give rise to **quantum turbulence**, providing a uniquely well-defined model system for studying turbulence with discrete, identical vortex structures.

### Topological Protection
Their quantized nature makes them topologically stable, meaning they cannot simply decay away continuously.

---

## Physical Systems Where Quantized Vortices Have Been Observed

| System | Notes |
|--------|-------|
| **Superfluid Helium-4** | The original system; vortices observed in the He II phase below 2.17 K. Bosonic superfluid. |
| **Superfluid Helium-3** | Fermionic superfluid (Cooper-paired ³He atoms) below ~2 mK; exhibits rich vortex structures due to complex order parameter. |
| **Atomic Bose-Einstein Condensates (BECs)** | Dilute ultracold gases (e.g., rubidium, sodium); vortices and lattices directly imaged since ~2000. |
| **Ultracold Fermionic Gases** | Paired fermionic atoms across the BEC-BCS crossover; vortex lattices demonstrated superfluidity. |
| **Superconductors** | Charged superfluids; magnetic flux enters as quantized **flux vortices** (Abrikosov lattice in type-II superconductors). |
| **Neutron Stars** | The neutron superfluid in the interior is believed to host vortices; their pinning and unpinning may explain pulsar **glitches**. |
| **Exciton-Polariton Condensates** | Driven-dissipative quantum fluids of light-matter quasiparticles in semiconductor microcavities. |

---

### Summary
Quantized vortices are the essential mechanism by which superfluids reconcile their irrotational, phase-coherent nature with rotation and angular momentum. They serve as a bridge between microscopic quantum mechanics and macroscopic fluid behavior, and their observation across such diverse systems—from laboratory quantum gases to astrophysical neutron stars—demonstrates the universality of superfluid physics.

# Vortices, Circulation, and Superfluidity

Superfluidity, first observed in liquid ⁴He below the lambda transition at approximately 2.17 K, represents a macroscopic quantum state characterized by the frictionless flow of a coherent condensate described by a complex order parameter ψ(**r**) = |ψ|e^(iφ). The superfluid velocity is directly proportional to the gradient of the macroscopic phase, **v**_s = (ℏ/m)∇φ, where m is the mass of the constituent particles. A fundamental consequence of this relation is that the flow is irrotational (∇ × **v**_s = 0) throughout the bulk, yet the superfluid can sustain rotation through the formation of quantized vortices. Because the order parameter must remain single-valued, the circulation around any closed contour enclosing a vortex core is quantized in units of κ = h/m:

$$\oint \mathbf{v}_s \cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell} = \frac{\hbar}{m} \oint \nabla\phi \cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell} = \frac{2\pi\hbar}{m} n = n\kappa,$$

where n is an integer winding number. Each quantized vortex possesses a core of atomic dimensions (on the order of the healing length ξ) within which the condensate density vanishes and superfluidity is locally destroyed, surrounded by a circulating velocity field that decays as 1/r. In rotating systems, energetic considerations favor the nucleation of an array of singly quantized (n = 1) vortices—the Abrikosov lattice—rather than a single multiply quantized line, allowing the superfluid to mimic solid-body rotation on macroscopic scales. This framework, developed through the foundational work of Onsager, Feynman, and others, underpins our understanding of quantized circulation not only in liquid helium but also in superconductors, where analogous flux quantization arises, and in dilute atomic Bose–Einstein condensates, where individual vortices and their dynamics can be directly imaged and manipulated.
